## Mean, $\sigma$ Known {#sec-mean-sigma-known}

```{r}
#| label: setup-2-1
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Recognize when the $z$ method for one mean applies.
2. Construct and interpret a confidence interval for $\mu$ when $\sigma$ is known.
3. Carry out a $z$ test for $\mu$ in five steps and write the conclusion.

### Concept

Sometimes the population standard deviation $\sigma$ is known from a large
source, such as a census or many years of administrative records, while the
mean may have changed. For example, the spread of daily wages in an industry
is fairly stable, but the mean wage changes with prices and minimum-wage policy.

When $\sigma$ is known, Chapter 1 tells us that
$$
z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}
$$
follows the standard normal distribution, provided the population is normal or
$n \ge 30$. Both the confidence interval and the test use this result.

### Formulas and Conditions

**Conditions:** $\sigma$ is known; a random sample; the population is normal or $n \ge 30$.

**$(1-\alpha)100\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$**
$$
\bar{x} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$
For a 95% CI, $z_{0.975} = `r fmt(crit_z(.975), 3)`$; for a 99% CI, $z_{0.995} = `r fmt(crit_z(.995), 3)`$.

**Test statistic** for $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$
$$
z_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}
$$

| $H_1$ | Critical region |
|:---:|:---|
| $\mu \ne \mu_0$ | $z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha/2}$ or $z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}$ |
| $\mu < \mu_0$ | $z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha}$ |
| $\mu > \mu_0$ | $z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha}$ |

```{r}
#| label: ex-2-1
a_sigma <- 60; a_n <- 36; a_xbar <- 358.4; a_mu0 <- 380
a_se <- round(a_sigma / sqrt(a_n), 4)
a_z975 <- crit_z(0.975); a_z95 <- crit_z(0.95)
a_lo <- a_xbar - a_z975 * a_se; a_hi <- a_xbar + a_z975 * a_se
a_z <- round((a_xbar - a_mu0) / a_se, 3)
```

### Worked Example

**Worked Example 2.1.1.** From many years of Labour Force Survey records, the
standard deviation of the daily wage of construction workers in Chiang Mai is
$\sigma$ = `r a_sigma` baht. A labour union surveys `r a_n` workers and finds a
mean daily wage of $\bar{x}$ = `r a_xbar` baht (hypothetical figures). The
Ministry of Labour reports a mean of `r a_mu0` baht; the union believes the true
mean is lower.

(a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean daily wage.
(b) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the mean daily wage is less than `r a_mu0` baht.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

**(a)** $n = `r a_n` \ge 30$, so the CLT applies.
$$
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{`r a_sigma`}{\sqrt{`r a_n`}} = `r num(a_se)`
$$
$$
\bar{x} \pm z_{0.975}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
= `r a_xbar` \pm `r fmt(a_z975, 3)`(`r num(a_se)`)
= `r a_xbar` \pm `r num(a_z975 * a_se)`
$$
95% CI: (`r fmt(a_lo, 2)`, `r fmt(a_hi, 2)`)

We are 95% confident that the mean daily wage of construction workers in Chiang
Mai is between `r fmt(a_lo, 2)` and `r fmt(a_hi, 2)` baht.

**(b)**

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: \mu = `r a_mu0`$ $\quad H_1: \mu < `r a_mu0`$

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.**
$$
z_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}
= \frac{`r a_xbar` - `r a_mu0`}{`r num(a_se)`} = `r fmt(a_z, 3)`
$$

**Step 4: Critical value and critical region.** Left-sided test, area 0.05 to
the left: $z_{0.05} = -z_{0.95} = `r fmt(-a_z95, 3)`$.
Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-a_z95, 3)`$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex-2-1
#| fig-cap: "Critical region for Worked Example 2.1.1"
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center
crit_plot("z", "left")
```

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.**
$z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(a_z, 3)`$ falls in the critical region
($`r fmt(a_z, 3)` < `r fmt(-a_z95, 3)`$), so we reject $H_0$.
That is, the mean daily wage of construction workers in Chiang Mai is less than
`r a_mu0` baht at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::

```{r}
#| label: yt-2-1
b_sigma <- 12; b_n <- 49; b_xbar <- 214.6; b_mu0 <- 210
b_se <- round(b_sigma / sqrt(b_n), 4)
b_lo <- b_xbar - a_z975 * b_se; b_hi <- b_xbar + a_z975 * b_se
b_z <- round((b_xbar - b_mu0) / b_se, 3)
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 2.1.1

The standard deviation of the price of a 5-kg bag of jasmine rice across shops
is known to be $\sigma$ = `r b_sigma` baht. A price-monitoring agency checks
`r b_n` shops and finds a mean price of $\bar{x}$ = `r b_xbar` baht
(hypothetical figures).

(a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean price.
(b) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the mean price is different from `r b_mu0` baht.
:::

::: {.workspace lines="4"}
:::

::: {.workspace steps="full"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 2.1.1"}
**(a)** $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = `r b_sigma`/\sqrt{`r b_n`} = `r num(b_se)`$;
$`r b_xbar` \pm `r fmt(a_z975, 3)`(`r num(b_se)`) = `r b_xbar` \pm `r num(a_z975 * b_se)`$.
95% CI: (`r fmt(b_lo, 2)`, `r fmt(b_hi, 2)`).
We are 95% confident that the mean price of a 5-kg bag of jasmine rice is between
`r fmt(b_lo, 2)` and `r fmt(b_hi, 2)` baht.

**(b)**

**Step 1.** $H_0: \mu = `r b_mu0` \quad H_1: \mu \ne `r b_mu0`$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $z_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{`r b_xbar` - `r b_mu0`}{`r num(b_se)`} = `r fmt(b_z, 3)`$

**Step 4.** $z_{0.025} = `r fmt(-a_z975, 3)`$, $z_{0.975} = `r fmt(a_z975, 3)`$.
Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-a_z975, 3)`$ or $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(a_z975, 3)`$.

**Step 5.** $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(b_z, 3)`$ falls in the critical region
($`r fmt(b_z, 3)` > `r fmt(a_z975, 3)`$), so we reject $H_0$.
That is, the mean price of a 5-kg bag of jasmine rice is different from
`r b_mu0` baht at the 0.05 level of significance; since $\bar{x}$ = `r b_xbar`,
the mean price is higher than `r b_mu0` baht.
:::

### Formula Summary

| | Formula |
|:---|:---|
| Conditions | $\sigma$ known; population normal or $n \ge 30$ |
| $(1-\alpha)100\%$ CI for $\mu$ | $\bar{x} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ |
| Test statistic | $z_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ |
| Critical region | $\ne$: $z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha/2}$ or $z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}$; $<$: $z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha}$; $>$: $z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha}$ |

```{r}
#| label: ex-2-1-exercises
e1_sigma <- 320; e1_n <- 64; e1_xbar <- 1240
e1_se <- round(e1_sigma / sqrt(e1_n), 4); e1_z <- crit_z(0.995)
e2_sigma <- 24; e2_n <- 40; e2_xbar <- 156.2; e2_mu0 <- 150
e2_se <- round(e2_sigma / sqrt(e2_n), 4); e2_z <- round((e2_xbar - e2_mu0) / e2_se, 3)
e3_sigma <- 12000; e3_n <- 100; e3_xbar <- 52100; e3_mu0 <- 50000
e3_se <- round(e3_sigma / sqrt(e3_n), 4); e3_z <- round((e3_xbar - e3_mu0) / e3_se, 3)
```

### Exercises

**2.1.1** Utility records show that the standard deviation of the monthly
electricity bill of households in a city is `r e1_sigma` baht. A sample of
`r e1_n` households has a mean bill of `r big(e1_xbar, 0)` baht (hypothetical
figures). Construct a 99% confidence interval for the mean monthly bill.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 2.1.1"}
$\sigma/\sqrt{n} = `r e1_sigma`/\sqrt{`r e1_n`} = `r num(e1_se)`$; $z_{0.995} = `r fmt(e1_z, 3)`$.
$`r e1_xbar` \pm `r fmt(e1_z, 3)`(`r num(e1_se)`) = `r e1_xbar` \pm `r num(e1_z * e1_se)`$.
99% CI: (`r big(e1_xbar - e1_z * e1_se)`, `r big(e1_xbar + e1_z * e1_se)`).
We are 99% confident that the mean monthly electricity bill is between
`r big(e1_xbar - e1_z * e1_se)` and `r big(e1_xbar + e1_z * e1_se)` baht.
:::

**2.1.2** A company claims that the mean monthly sales per salesperson are more
than `r e2_mu0` thousand baht. The standard deviation is known to be
`r e2_sigma` thousand baht. A sample of `r e2_n` salespeople has a mean of
`r e2_xbar` thousand baht (hypothetical figures). Test the claim at $\alpha$ = 0.01.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 2.1.2"}

**Step 1.** $H_0: \mu = `r e2_mu0` \quad H_1: \mu > `r e2_mu0`$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.01

**Step 3.** $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = `r e2_sigma`/\sqrt{`r e2_n`} = `r num(e2_se)`$;
$z_{\text{cal}} = (`r e2_xbar` - `r e2_mu0`)/`r num(e2_se)` = `r fmt(e2_z, 3)`$

**Step 4.** $z_{0.99} = `r fmt(crit_z(.99), 3)`$. Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(crit_z(.99), 3)`$.

**Step 5.** $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(e2_z, 3)`$ does not fall in the critical region
($`r fmt(e2_z, 3)` < `r fmt(crit_z(.99), 3)`$), so we accept $H_0$.
That is, the mean monthly sales per salesperson are equal to `r e2_mu0` thousand
baht at the 0.01 level of significance.
:::

**2.1.3** The standard deviation of savings deposits at a bank is known to be
`r big(e3_sigma, 0)` baht. A sample of `r e3_n` accounts has a mean balance of
`r big(e3_xbar, 0)` baht (hypothetical figures).

(a) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the mean balance is different from `r big(e3_mu0, 0)` baht.
(b) Construct a 95% CI for the mean balance. Does it agree with (a)?

::: {.answer title="Exercise 2.1.3"}
**(a)** $H_0: \mu = `r e3_mu0` \quad H_1: \mu \ne `r e3_mu0`$; $\alpha$ = 0.05.
$\sigma/\sqrt{n} = `r num(e3_se)`$;
$z_{\text{cal}} = (`r e3_xbar` - `r e3_mu0`)/`r num(e3_se)` = `r fmt(e3_z, 3)`$.
Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-a_z975, 3)`$ or $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(a_z975, 3)`$.
$z_{\text{cal}}$ does not fall in the critical region
($`r fmt(-a_z975, 3)` < `r fmt(e3_z, 3)` < `r fmt(a_z975, 3)`$), so we accept $H_0$.
That is, the mean balance is equal to `r big(e3_mu0, 0)` baht at the 0.05 level of significance.

**(b)** $`r e3_xbar` \pm `r fmt(a_z975, 3)`(`r num(e3_se)`)$:
95% CI (`r big(e3_xbar - a_z975 * e3_se)`, `r big(e3_xbar + a_z975 * e3_se)`).
The interval contains `r big(e3_mu0, 0)`, which agrees with accepting $H_0$ in (a).
:::
